title: Storage: why disk is slow and why files exist
story:
Memory forgets when the power goes. Storage does not, and everything unpleasant about storage follows from what it costs to have that property.

Patterson's numbers make the shape of the cost precise. Comparing a disk of 1983 with one of 2003: bandwidth improved from 0.6 to 86 megabytes per second, a factor of about 140, while latency improved only from 48.3 to 5.7 milliseconds, a factor of about 8. Twenty years of engineering made the pipe a hundred and forty times wider and the wait eight times shorter. He quotes David Clark on why that asymmetry is structural rather than a failure of effort: bandwidth problems can be cured with money, latency problems are harder because the speed of light is fixed — you cannot bribe God.

That asymmetry is the whole design constraint. If one access costs milliseconds and the transfer once started is fast, then the number of accesses dominates and their size barely matters. Reading a megabyte in one go is comparable to reading a kilobyte in one go, and enormously cheaper than reading a kilobyte a thousand times. Every sensible thing about storage design — block sizes, sequential layout, batching writes, the index structures two lessons from here — is a consequence of that single fact.

Then there is the question of what a program sees, and the answer everyone now takes for granted was a design decision. Among the features Ritchie and Thompson listed in 1974 were a hierarchical file system incorporating demountable volumes, and compatible file, device and inter-process input and output. The second is the important one: a program reads bytes from a thing, and the thing may be a stored file, a device, or another program, and the reading code does not change. A named sequence of bytes with open, read, write and close became the universal interface to persistence.

What that abstraction buys is obvious and what it hides is the lesson. It hides the block. It hides that the sequence you are treating as bytes is stored in chunks, and that touching two bytes in the same chunk is nearly free while touching two bytes in different chunks costs two accesses. It hides that the device has a minimum unit of work far larger than the unit your program is thinking in. Code that would be entirely reasonable against memory becomes pathological against storage, and the interface is identical in both cases — which is precisely why it is worth knowing what sits behind it.

problem.name: The storage gap
problem.shape: Data has to outlive the process, and the devices that make that possible are orders of magnitude further away in time than memory.
tell: a routine reads or writes many small items separately
the same total volume takes wildly different times to move
a loop issues one request per row
the access pattern is random and the device is a disk
problem.move: Count accesses rather than bytes. Batch small reads and writes into large ones, lay data out so that things used together are stored together, and let the block size rather than the record size drive the design. Where the pattern is genuinely random, expect to pay per access and budget for it.
problem.invariant: The cost of storage is dominated by the number of accesses, not their size, because latency has improved by a factor of eight where bandwidth has improved by a factor of a hundred and forty.
problem.breaks: The file abstraction is uniform and the cost underneath is not. A program addressing bytes cannot see the block boundaries it is crossing, so the same interface serves an access pattern that is nearly free and one that is catastrophic, with nothing in the code to distinguish them.

cost.time: one access costs on the order of milliseconds, which is millions of instructions
cost.space: blocks are read whole, so serving one byte can move thousands
cost.beats: addressing the device directly, which every program would then have to know how to do, and keeping everything in memory, which does not survive the power going out

worked.problem: Why can reading the same number of bytes take vastly different amounts of time?
worked.reasoning:
Because the bytes are not what you are charged for. You are charged for accesses, and the same volume can be one access or a hundred thousand.

The measurements make the ratio concrete. Between 1983 and 2003, disk bandwidth improved by a factor of about 140 — from 0.6 to 86 megabytes per second — while latency improved by a factor of about 8, from 48.3 to 5.7 milliseconds. So a request has a large fixed cost and a small marginal one. Once the transfer has started it is fast; getting it started is the expensive part.

Follow that through. A megabyte read sequentially is one access plus a fast transfer. The same megabyte read as a thousand scattered kilobyte requests is a thousand fixed costs, and the transfer time is nearly irrelevant to the total. Same bytes, same device, orders of magnitude apart — and the two pieces of code differ only in the order they ask for things.

The reason the asymmetry is structural rather than a gap somebody will close is worth saying, because it tells you the trade is permanent. Bandwidth problems can be cured with money; latency problems are harder because the speed of light is fixed. Adding width is an engineering purchase. Reducing delay runs into physics.

What follows practically is that you count accesses rather than bytes. Batch small writes into large ones. Store things that are read together next to each other, so that one access serves them all. Read ahead when the pattern is predictable, since bandwidth is the cheap resource and speculating with it to avoid a wait is exactly the right trade. And design around the block: the device has a minimum unit of work, and two items in the same block are nearly free together while two in different blocks cost double.

The part that makes this a genuine trap rather than an obvious point is that the file interface hides all of it. A program addresses a sequence of bytes and cannot see the block boundaries it is crossing, so identical-looking code performs entirely differently depending on layout. Which is why the uniform interface is both the thing that makes storage usable and the thing that makes its cost invisible.

problem.practice: Write a million small records to a file one at a time, then write the same million batched into large blocks, and time both. Then read them back in stored order and in shuffled order and time those. Four numbers, one device, and only the access pattern changed.

beats.broke: The persistent store is far away in time terms and is addressed in blocks, not in the bytes and structures a program actually holds.
beats.fix: Put a uniform abstraction over it — a named sequence of bytes that can be opened, read, written and closed — so programs address data by name while the system handles blocks, devices and placement.
beats.cost: The uniformity hides the access cost, so code that would be reasonable in memory becomes pathological against a device where one access costs millions of instructions.

interview.q: Why can reading the same number of bytes take vastly different amounts of time?
interview.trap: Reasoning about the volume of data. Volume is the cheap part — the charge is per access, and the same megabyte can be one access or a thousand depending only on the order the program asks for it.

takeaway: Storage charges per access rather than per byte — twenty years made the pipe 140 times wider and the wait only 8 times shorter — and the file abstraction that makes it usable is exactly what hides the block boundaries doing the charging.
